text: A trapeze artist accepts a marriage proposal she has no intention of honoring, and the people around her are paying closer attention than she knows. Sixty-four minutes is a short run even for 1932, and Tod Browning spends almost none of it on suspense machinery; the courtship, the money, and the arithmetic of an inheritance are laid out early and plainly. What fills the rest is company life. The sideshow performers eat together, argue, work, and keep their own counsel, filmed at the level of ordinary labor rather than display, so that the scheme running above them starts to look like the deviant thing. It sits in the National Film Registry now. By the time the wedding arrives, the audience has been taught whose house this is.

Everything here runs on one substance that exists in a single place in the universe, which is less a plot device than a description of how empires choose their wars. Denis Villeneuve takes 155 minutes and declines to hurry: the scale is enormous, the talk is quiet, and long stretches go to travel, weather, and machinery moving across open ground. Paul Atreides is sent to the most dangerous planet there is carrying a destiny nobody has fully explained to him, and the film is patient about how little his family name does for him once he is standing on the sand. What holds all of it together is the proposition the story keeps returning to, that survival belongs to whoever can master fear, treated not as a slogan but as a practical difficulty, managed hour by hour and never quite solved.

The dictator in this picture is called Adenoid Hynkel, and the year stamped on it is 1940, which is most of the gamble in two facts. Charlie Chaplin builds the thing on a split: an empire being enlarged from a palace by a man in love with his own voice, and a poor Jewish barber trying to stay beneath the notice of that same regime. The comedy is physical and exact, never softened into whimsy, and the war material is not a backdrop for the jokes but the reason they have to land. What is strange now is how little of the humor depends on knowing how any of it turned out; the ridicule works on posture, on ceremony, on the appetite for applause. It runs 125 minutes, takes both halves seriously, and lets the barber's ordinary problem of going unnoticed carry as much weight as the palace.

A private security firm sets up on a middle-class street in Recife and begins charging residents for a protection nobody has agreed is needed. Kleber Mendonça Filho gives that arrangement 131 minutes, long enough for the real subject to surface: who works for whom on this block, which door a delivery is expected to use, what a night watchman is worth in cash. It is filed as a thriller and the label is not wrong, though the menace comes less from any crime than from the layout itself, apartments above and houses behind and gates that lock regardless of who is guarding them. The Abraccine list of the hundred best Brazilian films keeps it, and the placement makes sense: most films would explain a street like this. This one lets it stand and waits.

In 1902, on a sea island off the coast of South Carolina, a family is packing to leave for the North, and the film stays with the preparations rather than the departure. Julie Dash shoots the day closer to memory than to reportage: relatives arranged in the frame as if for a photograph, cloth and water and hair given as much attention as dialogue, generations talking past one another about what the move will cost. An island keeps things a mainland will not, and that is the pressure here, in what travels north, what is left where it is, and who gets to decide. It sits on the Sight & Sound Critics' Poll. Across 112 minutes nothing is hurried, and an ordinary meal is filmed with the gravity usually reserved for an event.

A girl turns nine, and her family informs her that the terms of her life change today. Three episodes, seventy-four minutes, and no attempt to braid them into a single plot: next comes a woman pedaling in a race her husband has forbidden, then an old woman spending on everything she was never given. Marziyeh Meshkiny lets the arrangement carry the argument, childhood and marriage and old age set side by side as three stations on one road rather than three separate grievances, and keeps the telling plain enough that no rule ever has to be stated aloud. The comedy in it is dry and real and never at the expense of the women it follows. A bicycle is a bicycle and also a verdict. It is short by feature standards, and not a minute goes to explaining itself.

A boy who bullied other boys is dead, and it is his father going from classmate to classmate asking for an account. The reversal runs the film: the person owed sympathy is the one everybody has reason to resent, and the answers come from teenagers who have not yet decided what they are willing to say out loud. Yoon Sung-hyun works with a small cast, school corridors, and 117 minutes in which no adult is permitted to explain anything. What the film is exact about is the way a friendship between boys polices itself, the joke that goes one degree too far, the loyalty that holds only as long as the group does, the injury that cannot be admitted without ending everything. Most of the time it looks like ordinary afternoons.

Qasem's job with the municipality is to clear the street of the people selling on it, and he goes home to a marriage that is not holding either. Eighty-one minutes, one city, and a man trying to improve his position by exactly the means available to him: a municipal wage, a favor owed, an arrangement made with money that is not his. The authority he holds on the pavement is precisely the kind he has none of at home, and Narges is the one who has to sit and hear the reasoning. Mohsen Gharaie keeps the camera at the height of doorways and counters, close to the transactions themselves, and declines to sort anyone into right and wrong. What is left is the daily accounting of a man who is not cruel and is not doing well.

A location scout spends a day with the art director on her project, and what the film cares about is what survives of that day afterward. Sixty-eight minutes leaves no room for a second storyline and none is attempted; the meeting, and then the distance from it, is the entire structure. Nawapol Thamrongrattanarit is working on the equipment of memory here, the record kept for professional reasons, the file that outlives the feeling it was meant to hold, the difference between retrieving an afternoon and being able to feel it again. Two people talking about locations and work is small material by design, since small material is what nobody thinks to keep until it has gone. A New Currents award came of it. Nothing in the film is raised in volume.

Ròm is fourteen, and his trade is carrying lottery bets between people who have nothing and the numbers that might change that. Seventy-nine minutes, filed as action as much as drama, which suits a life conducted at a sprint: the money moves, the boy moves faster, and the gap between the two is what he lives on. Trần Thanh Huy keeps the stakes domestic rather than criminal, since Ròm is not building anything but saving toward the fare and the address that would let him find his parents. That produces an odd sort of tension, the danger being less a rival or a raid than the arithmetic of a boy trying to accumulate anything at all while living unsettled. The chase is toward an address he does not yet have.

The apartment holds a woman in her thirties, a cat, and a routine that asks nothing of anybody. Jeong-hye works a window at the post office, eats lunch with the women from her shift, and goes home; ninety-nine minutes are spent watching a life arranged so that nothing ever needs explaining. Lee Yoon-ki films it without irony and without pity, which is rarer than it sounds, and lets the smallest deviation register as an event: a customer who lingers, an aspiring writer who takes an interest, a silence held one beat past comfortable. The Blue Dragon Film Award for Best New Actress was earned in what the performance withholds. The film is more interested in Jeong-hye's privacy than in an explanation, and never forces one out of her.

A girl is missing, and the school settles with alarming speed on which of her classmates ought to answer for it. What follows is less an investigation than a demonstration: teachers, police, and grieving parents each need an account, and the schoolgirl they have chosen cannot produce one. Kim Ui-seok holds 113 minutes at the pitch of an interrogation, rooms and corridors and the same question repeated until the answers begin to serve the questioner, so that the mystery label describes the pressure rather than any puzzle waiting to be solved. The cruelty is procedural. Nobody administering it believes they are doing harm, and the film declines to hand out the relief of a verdict on whether the accusation was fair.

A filmmaker is documenting a tragedy her community has not finished arguing over, and the standards she is applying to other people turn out to be available for use on her. Yujiro Harumoto takes 152 minutes with this, long for a chamber piece and right for the subject, because the method is accumulation: interviews, permissions, promises made to people who will have to live with the result. The moral question is never posed in the abstract. It arrives as a decision about one particular person on one particular afternoon, with a camera already running and a reputation on the table. What makes it uncomfortable is how reasonable each compromise looks by itself. The weighing gets done in ordinary rooms, by people who consider themselves fair.
